feedback.silentdefault: Right. A screen reader narrates two things by default: whatever currently has focus, and content a user explicitly navigates to or requests read. A DOM node updating elsewhere on the page, with focus still parked on the dropdown, produces no automatic announcement — that's not a bug, it's the baseline behavior, and it's exactly why live regions exist as an opt-in mechanism.
feedback.bug: No screen reader bug here — this is universal, expected behavior across every screen reader, not a defect in one specific tool.

contentSections.mechanism: **Silence is the default for anything outside current focus.** A sighted user's peripheral vision catches the price change without looking directly at it; a screen reader user has no equivalent — they hear only what they're currently "looking" at (focus) or what they've explicitly asked to have read. Making a dynamic update audible requires deliberately marking the region that changes as live: `aria-live="polite"` (announce when convenient, waiting for a pause) or `aria-live="assertive"` (interrupt and announce immediately, reserved for things that genuinely can't wait — an error that blocks submission, a session about to expire). Without one of those, or without moving focus to the changed content directly, the update simply never reaches the user.

contentSections.body: `role="status"` and `role="alert"` are shorthand ARIA roles that imply `aria-live="polite"` and `"assertive"` respectively — both are legitimate, choose based on whether waiting for the user to be idle is acceptable (status) or the update genuinely can't wait (alert).
An update happening with focus somewhere else is invisible to a screen reader user by default — audibility has to be built in deliberately, it's never automatic.

contentSections.title: Live regions can also go wrong the other direction

contentSections.body: A stock-trading dashboard marks its entire price ticker as `aria-live="assertive"`. Every price tick — dozens per second — interrupts whatever the screen reader was doing to announce a number nobody asked to hear right now, making the rest of the page unusable for anything else.

contentSections.code: AAPL $187.42 MSFT $412.05
contentSections.question: What's the actual problem with marking this container aria-live="assertive"?

options.label: Assertive live regions interrupt whatever the screen reader is currently saying, so constant updates make the page unusable for anything else — this should be polite at most, and probably shouldn't be a blanket live region on the whole container at all
aria-live only works on <span> elements, not <div>, so this markup does nothing
Nothing is wrong — traders need real-time information and assertive is the only setting fast enough

feedback.toonoisy: Right, and a genuinely common real-world overcorrection: a team learns live regions announce updates and decides more urgency is better, marking something assertive that fires constantly — producing an experience arguably worse than the original silence, because the screen reader is now being talked over every few seconds by content the user often didn't ask about right now.
feedback.wrongtag: aria-live works on any element type — that's not the defect here.
feedback.nothingwrong: "Assertive" doesn't mean "faster" — it means "interrupt current speech." A torrent of interruptions is the opposite of usable. A genuinely time-critical single alert (a stop-loss trigger firing) might deserve assertive; a whole scrolling ticker doesn't.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Live regions are for a single, meaningful update someone needs to know about without hunting for it — a form error, a save confirmation, a chat message arriving. Applying one to a fast-changing, high-volume region turns a helpful feature into a wall of noise, and "assertive" specifically means every one of those updates cuts off whatever the user was already listening to, including the screen reader trying to read something else they'd actually asked for.

contentSections.body: A working rule before adding any live region: is this a discrete event a user needs told about, or continuous data they'd check when they want to? Continuous, high-frequency data — tickers, live counters, a progress percentage updating several times a second — generally shouldn't be a blanket live region. A periodic summary, or a live region that only fires on a meaningful threshold crossing, serves the same need without the noise.

A missing live region makes an update invisible; an overused one makes everything else unlistenable — both are diagnosable from the same question: does this update genuinely need to interrupt right now?

title: Lab — Complete a Purchase Flow With the Screen Reader Alone
description: Turn the monitor away and complete a real, multi-step flow using only what the screen reader tells you — transcribing exactly what's announced, and marking every point where it goes silent, wrong, or unclear.

learningObjectives.text: Complete a multi-step flow using only a screen reader's output to decide what to do next
Transcribe a screen-reader session with the precision a developer needs to reproduce a gap unassisted
Diagnose each silent or wrong announcement to its most likely mechanism

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Turn your monitor off, or angle it away if that's what's realistic today. Every line in this transcript has to survive the test "is this literally what I heard," not "I'm fairly sure this is what it would have said."

contentSections.title: Screen-reader-only purchase flow transcript
contentSections.brief: Pick a real, multi-step purchase or signup flow you can access today — an online store checkout, a subscription signup, a ticket booking. Turn on NVDA with Chrome or VoiceOver with Safari, whichever you have access to. Turn your monitor off or look away from it if you can manage that safely; if that's not realistic today, the rule that actually matters is not looking at the screen to decide what to do next, only to type when you need to see the keyboard. Complete the entire flow using only what the screen reader tells you, and write down literally what gets announced at each step, in order.
contentSections.deliverable: A step-by-step transcript: what was announced (or what silence you got instead) at each point in the flow, with every gap flagged and its likely cause named — missing accessible name, missing or misused live region, unhelpful heading structure, or a custom control missing the ARIA wiring its behavior needed.

stages.title: Set up and choose the flow
stages.instructions: Pick a flow with at least four real steps (browse or select → cart or details → some form of checkout → a final success state). Turn on NVDA+Chrome or VoiceOver+Safari — whichever you have access to. Decide now, before you start, that you won't glance at the screen to figure out what to do next — the same commitment the keyboard lab asked for with the mouse.
stages.checkpoint: You've named the flow, the screen reader/browser pairing, and committed to navigating by ear.

stages.title: Walk the flow, writing down every announcement
stages.instructions: Move through the flow using only the screen reader's output to decide what to do next. At each step, write down literally what you heard — the actual words, not a paraphrase — including anything that felt wrong, confusing, or didn't match what you'd expect from having seen the page before. The moment something changes with no announcement at all (a price, a validation state, a step counter), note what you know changed and mark it as silent.
stages.checkpoint: You have a step-by-step transcript covering the whole flow, including every silent gap you noticed.

stages.title: Diagnose each gap to a likely cause
stages.instructions: For every silent or wrong announcement, name the most likely mechanism from this module: missing accessible name, missing or misused live region, a heading structure that gave you no useful orientation, or a custom control missing the ARIA wiring its keyboard behavior needed. Where you're genuinely unsure, say so rather than guessing a cause that doesn't fit — an honest "unclear, needs a developer to check the markup" is a legitimate line in a real audit.
stages.checkpoint: Every transcript gap has either a named likely cause or an honest note that the cause isn't clear from testing alone.

stages.title: Order by what it cost the task, and self-check
stages.instructions: Order your findings by what actually happened to your ability to complete the flow — did a gap stop you outright, force you to guess, or just cost a moment of confusion? Then run the self-check against the rubric below before calling this done.
stages.checkpoint: Findings are ordered by real cost to task completion, and the transcript would let someone else understand exactly what you heard without needing to be there.

rubric.criterion: The flow was actually completed screen-reader-only
rubric.meets: Every step attempted using only what the screen reader announced to decide what to do, not glancing at the screen to figure out where to click.

rubric.criterion: The transcript records what was actually said, not a summary
rubric.meets: Specific announced text is quoted or closely paraphrased, not reduced to "it announced the button correctly" with no detail.

rubric.criterion: Every silent gap is marked, not just the ones that blocked you
rubric.meets: Minor gaps that didn't stop the task are recorded alongside major ones, not filtered out for feeling small.

rubric.criterion: A likely cause is named for each gap, or an honest "unclear" is given
rubric.meets: No gap is left with no explanation at all, and no cause is guessed just to have something to write.

rubric.criterion: Severity reflects what the gap cost the actual task
rubric.meets: A gap that stopped the flow entirely and one that was just mildly disorienting are rated in the right relative order.

contentSections.body: A flow that "sounds fine" skimmed with your eyes and the screen reader running in the background is not the same as a flow you've actually completed by ear — this lab is the difference.

Insert+Down Arrow — it reads the whole page from the top
Tab — it moves to the next interactive element

The page's JavaScript has disabled the screen reader

This is a bug specific to that screen reader

title: What the browser exposes, and to whom
description: The browser builds a third tree alongside the DOM and the render tree — the accessibility tree — and it, not the HTML source, is what every screen reader actually reads from.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what the accessibility tree is and how it differs from the DOM
Describe the pipeline from HTML to accessibility tree to platform API to screen reader
Identify what a screen reader can and can't access about an element

contentSections.title: The tree browsers build for exactly this purpose

contentSections.body: A developer insists a button "has no accessibility issues" because it renders correctly and clicks correctly with a mouse. They've never heard of the accessibility tree — a completely separate structure the browser builds specifically for assistive technology, sitting parallel to the DOM tree and the render tree they already know about.

contentSections.question: Browsers already build a DOM tree (structure) and a render tree (what's painted). Do they build a third tree, specifically for assistive technology?
contentSections.answer: Yes — the accessibility tree. Every browser computes it from the DOM plus computed ARIA and semantics, and it's what NVDA, JAWS and VoiceOver actually read from — not the DOM directly, and not the rendered pixels.
contentSections.hint: Think about what a screen reader needs that neither raw HTML source nor rendered pixels alone would give it — a role, an accessible name, a current state.

contentSections.body: The pipeline: HTML/DOM plus ARIA attributes and computed visibility → the browser computes an accessibility tree (nodes with a role, a name, a value, and states) → that tree is exposed through a platform accessibility API (UI Automation on Windows, AXAPI on macOS, AT-SPI on Linux) → assistive technology — a screen reader, switch access, voice control — reads from that API, not from the HTML source directly. This is exactly why viewing page source doesn't tell you what will actually be announced; you have to inspect the computed tree, which is what the last lesson in this module walks through in devtools.

Some elements are removed from the accessibility tree entirely, not just hidden visually: `display: none` and `visibility: hidden` remove a node and everything nested inside it, from both the screen and the tree. `aria-hidden="true"` does something narrower and more surprising — it removes a node and its descendants from the accessibility tree while leaving them completely visible on screen. That's a real, sometimes intentional pattern (hiding a decorative icon that duplicates adjacent visible text), and also a genuinely common source of bugs: apply it to a container that turns out to hold a real interactive control, and that control becomes invisible to a screen reader while a sighted user can see and click it perfectly well.
The accessibility tree is a real, separate structure the browser computes — not the HTML source, not the rendered pixels — and it's the only thing a screen reader ever actually reads.

contentSections.title: What actually gets exposed for a control

contentSections.body: Two buttons look pixel-identical. One announces "Add to cart, button." The other announces just "button," with nothing else. To a sighted user they're indistinguishable. To a screen reader user, one of them is unusable.

contentSections.scenario: A button contains only an SVG icon and no visible text: `<button><svg>...</svg></button>`, with nothing else supplied.
contentSections.question: What does a screen reader announce for it?

options.label: Whatever the SVG's internal <title> says, if present — otherwise nothing meaningful, likely just "button"
"Icon button" — screen readers describe icon-only controls generically
The image filename referenced by the icon

feedback.svgtitle: Right, broadly — an SVG's own <title> element can contribute to the accessible name if referenced correctly, but with nothing supplied at all, there's no text anywhere in the accessible-name computation to find, and the control announces with no meaningful name.
feedback.iconbutton: "Icon button" isn't real text anyone wrote — screen readers don't invent descriptive labels. They report exactly what's actually exposed as the accessible name, which for bare SVG with nothing supplied is empty.
feedback.filename: Filenames play no part in accessible-name computation for inline SVG at all — that's not one of the sources the algorithm checks.

contentSections.concept: **Accessible name computation is a real, specified algorithm, not a guess.** Roughly, in priority order: `aria-labelledby`, then `aria-label`, then native labeling (a `<label>`, an `alt` attribute, a `<caption>`), then visible text content. An icon-only button with none of those supplies nothing at any step, and a screen reader either announces just its role ("button") or, in some cases, nothing recognizable at all — which is exactly the gap the next lesson in this module goes into in full.

contentSections.body: This is worth internalizing early: "accessible name" isn't a vague sense of what a control is about — it's the specific output of a defined algorithm, checked in a fixed order, and a control either has one from that computation or it doesn't. Nothing about how obvious the control's purpose looks on screen changes what that algorithm actually finds.
The accessible name isn't inferred from how a control looks — it's the output of a specific, ordered computation, and an icon with nothing supplying text to that computation gets nothing back.

title: Native elements versus div with a click handler
description: A div has no implicit role at all — pixel-identical to a real control, and structurally invisible as one, until the specific work of adding it back is actually done.

learningObjectives.text: Compare what a native interactive element exposes automatically versus a div
Diagnose the accessibility-tree difference between two pixel-identical controls
Decide what a div-based custom control genuinely needs to represent itself correctly

contentSections.title: Same pixels, different tree nodes

contentSections.body:
Two "Save" buttons — one ``, one `
Save
` — are byte-for-byte identical on screen, same font, same padding, same hover state. Opening the accessibility tree in devtools shows one node as role "button," name "Save." The other shows up with no interactive role at all.

contentSections.scenario: The two Save buttons above, one native, one a styled div with an onclick handler.
contentSections.question: What does the accessibility tree show for the div-based version?

options.label: role: generic (or none) — no interactive semantics at all, despite having an onclick handler and visible text
role: button, because the visible text says "Save"
role: link, because clickable divs default to link semantics

feedback.generic: Right. A div has no implicit ARIA role — the browser doesn't infer "button" from an onclick handler or from text content that happens to read like a button label. It exposes exactly what the tag actually means, which for a bare div is nothing interactive.
feedback.inferbutton: Text content never determines role — the algorithm that computes accessible *name* reads text content, but role comes from the element (or an explicit ARIA role), and a div carries neither.
feedback.link: There's no such default. Clicking behavior added by JavaScript changes what happens on click, never what the accessibility tree exposes as the element's role.

contentSections.mechanism: **This is the DOM-versus-tree distinction from the last lesson, made concrete.** The tree reflects semantic markup — the actual element and any explicit ARIA — never behavior wired up in JavaScript. A handful of native elements carry an implicit role for free: `<button>` → button, `<a href>` → link, `<input type="checkbox">` → checkbox, `<select>` → combobox or listbox. A `<div>` or `<span>` carries none of them, no matter what class, click handler, or visible text is attached — every one of those roles has to be added back explicitly with `role="..."` if you build the control from a div instead.

contentSections.body: This matters beyond one Save button: any component library built primarily from styled divs — a very common pattern in design-system-heavy codebases, because divs are the most flexible thing to style — starts from zero on semantics for every single control, every time, whether or not anyone remembers to add it back.
A div carries no implicit role, ever — not from its class, not from an onclick handler, not from text content that reads like a label. Every one of those has to be added back by hand.

contentSections.title: When building a custom control is actually worth the semantics work

contentSections.body: A design system team is proposing a custom multi-select tag input — type a name, pick from a filtered list, selected tags appear as removable chips. There's a genuine visual requirement here a native `<select multiple>` can't meet. The question is what representing it correctly in the accessibility tree actually requires.

contentSections.scenario: The proposed multi-select tag input, built from styled divs and a text input.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuinely necessary for the accessibility tree to represent this control correctly?

items.label: aria-multiselectable="true", since more than one tag can be selected
aria-selected on each option, reflecting whether it's currently chosen
A decorative background-color change on hover
Managed focus (roving tabindex or aria-activedescendant) so arrow keys move through options without leaving the text input
A console.log statement recording every selection for debugging

explanation.listbox: Necessary — this is what tells assistive technology the suggestions container is a list of selectable options, not generic decorative content.
explanation.multiselectable: Necessary — without it, a screen reader has no way to know more than one option can be active at once, which changes how a user would expect to interact with it.
explanation.selected: Necessary — this is the "value" a listbox owes per option: which ones are currently chosen, kept in sync every time selection changes.
explanation.bgcolor: Purely visual, and irrelevant to the accessibility tree — hover styling changes nothing about what's announced or how the control operates.
explanation.roving: Necessary — without managed focus, arrow keys either do nothing or move real DOM focus off the text input, breaking the ability to keep typing while browsing suggestions (the same combobox mechanism from the screen reader module).
explanation.consolelog: A debugging aid with zero effect on anything a user, sighted or not, ever experiences.

contentSections.synthesis: Four of these six are genuinely load-bearing for the accessibility tree; two are irrelevant to it entirely. That ratio is roughly what a real custom control costs to represent correctly — real, specific, learnable work, not an open-ended unknown, which is exactly the kind of thing worth naming plainly when deciding whether a custom control's visual requirement is worth taking on.

contentSections.body: A custom control's accessibility cost isn't vague — it's a specific, enumerable list of role, state and focus-management work, and naming that list is what turns "is this worth it" into an answerable question.

title: Name, role, value: the three things every control owes
description: Every control owes an accessible name, a role, and a current value or state — and each one can be missing or wrong completely independently of the other two.

learningObjectives.text: State the accessible name computation's priority order
Diagnose a missing or wrong name/role/value on a real control
Fix a broken control by supplying whichever of the three is actually missing

contentSections.title: Accessible name: where it actually comes from

contentSections.body: A form has `<label>Email</label><input type="text">` with no `for`/`id` connecting them. Visually the label sits right next to the field — it looks perfectly labeled. The accessible name computation finds nothing programmatically associated, and the input announces as just "edit text," with no name at all.

contentSections.problem: Diagnose the disconnected label and fix it.

steps.label: Check for a programmatic association
steps.work: Look for a matching `for`/`id` pair, or the input nested directly inside the `<label>`.
steps.why: Visual adjacency means nothing to the accessible-name computation — it only follows an explicit, coded association.

steps.label: Confirm none exists
steps.work: The label has no `for` attribute, the input has no matching `id`, and the input isn't nested inside the label.
steps.why: This rules out the possibility that it's associated some other valid way and confirms the actual gap.

steps.label: Name the actual defect
steps.work: The label text exists in the DOM and reads correctly to a sighted user, but is not programmatically connected to the field it visually labels.
steps.why: Distinguishing "label text is missing" from "label text exists but isn't connected" points a developer at the actual one-line fix instead of a rewrite.

steps.label: State the fix
steps.work: Add a matching `for`/`id` pair, or nest the input inside the label, or add `aria-labelledby` pointing at the label's `id`.
steps.why: Any of the three creates the missing programmatic association; which one to use is mostly a matter of which is least disruptive to the existing markup.

faded.problem: A second field has the for/id association done correctly — but also carries an `aria-label="Contact info"` attribute left over from an earlier version of the form.

blanks.prompt: Given both a correct native label and an aria-label with different text are present, which one wins the accessible name? (name the attribute)
blanks.why: aria-label sits higher in the accessible-name computation's priority order than native label association — it wins even when the native label is completely correct.

blanks.prompt: What does a screen reader user actually hear for this field?
blanks.why: That's the literal winning value from the computation — not "Email," even though "Email" is the label a sighted user reads right next to the field.

blanks.prompt: What kind of bug does this represent — new, or leftover? (one word)
blanks.why: This is a very common real pattern: an aria-label added at some earlier point (maybe when there was no visible label at all) silently outlives the reason it was added, and nobody removes it once a proper visible label goes in.

contentSections.procedure: **The accessible name computation checks sources in a fixed priority order — `aria-labelledby`, then `aria-label`, then native labeling (label association, alt, caption), then visible text content — and stops at the first one it finds.** A correct native label further down that order never gets a chance to matter if something higher up is present, even if that higher-priority value is wrong, stale, or contradicts what's visually on screen.

contentSections.body: aria-label overrides a correct native label if both are present — a leftover aria-label from earlier markup can silently defeat a properly connected label added later.

contentSections.title: Role and value: the other two things a control owes

contentSections.body: Recall the custom toggle switch from the keyboard module — a div fixed with `tabindex="0"` and a keydown handler for Space, so it's now genuinely operable by keyboard. It still only announces as "clickable." A screen reader user has no idea it's a toggle, or whether it's currently on.

contentSections.scenario: The fixed toggle: tabindex="0" present, Space key toggles it, but no role or aria-checked attribute anywhere.
contentSections.question: What's still missing?

options.label: role="switch" (or checkbox), and aria-checked reflecting the current state — role, and value, on top of the keyboard fix
Nothing — key handling was the only remaining piece
Just an aria-label naming the control

feedback.roleandvalue: Right. This control now has operability (focusable, Space activates it) but still owes two of the three things every control owes: a role saying what kind of control this is, and a value saying what state it's currently in. Without both, a screen reader user hears something clickable with no idea it's a two-state switch or which state it's in.
feedback.nothing: Keyboard operability and screen reader representation are two entirely separate axes of "working" — this control genuinely passes a keyboard-only test now and still fails a screen reader test completely.
feedback.namealone: A name alone (assuming the visible text already provides one) still leaves role and value both missing — hearing "Dark mode, clickable" tells you nothing about it being a toggle or its current state.

contentSections.concept: **Name, role and value are three separate obligations, and a control can satisfy any combination of them independently.** "Value" isn't only for form fields with a literal typed value — for a checkbox or switch it's `aria-checked` (true/false/mixed); for a slider it's `aria-valuenow`/`min`/`max`; for a combobox it's the currently selected option plus `aria-expanded`. Whatever kind of control it is, "what state is it in right now" is information a native element reports automatically and a custom one has to maintain by hand, updated every time the state actually changes.

contentSections.body: This is the same three-part model the keyboard module used for focusability, key handling and semantics — restated for what specifically gets exposed to a screen reader rather than what a sighted keyboard user can reach. A broken custom control in a real audit almost always has exactly one or two of {name, role, value} missing, not all three — which one narrows the fix from "rebuild this" to a specific, small change.
Name, role and value are three separate things a control owes, and diagnosing which one is actually missing is what turns a vague "this doesn't work with a screen reader" into an actionable finding.

title: ARIA that helps, and ARIA that overrides something correct
description: ARIA can override an element's correct native semantics — and when it does, the result isn't neutral, it's actively worse than having added nothing at all.

learningObjectives.text: Explain how ARIA attributes can override a native element's correct semantics
Diagnose a case where ARIA makes an accessibility outcome worse, not better
State the "no ARIA is better than bad ARIA" principle and when it applies

contentSections.title: ARIA can override something that was already right

contentSections.body: A financial dashboard's actual data table — rows and columns of quarterly figures, real `<th>` header cells — gets `role="presentation"` added to its `<table>` tag, copy-pasted from a layout table pattern elsewhere in the codebase that genuinely was just for visual alignment, not real data.

contentSections.scenario: The real data table above, now carrying role="presentation" by mistake.
contentSections.question: What happens to a screen reader user navigating this table now?

options.label: They lose header, row and column announcement and navigation entirely — the table announces as generic content, not tabular data
Nothing changes — role="presentation" only affects sighted styling
The table becomes keyboard-inaccessible

feedback.loseall: Right. role="presentation" (and its synonym role="none") tells the browser to expose an element and its required owned elements as if they carried no semantic role at all — powerful and correct for a genuine layout table, actively harmful applied to real tabular data, because it strips exactly the row/column/header relationships a table-navigation command depends on.
feedback.nochange: The visual styling is completely untouched — this is purely an accessibility-tree change, invisible to a sighted user, which is exactly why it can survive a design review and a QA pass done only by looking at the screen.
feedback.keyboard: Keyboard behavior (Tab order, any focusable cells) is unaffected by this role change — this is specifically about what a screen reader announces, not what a keyboard can reach.

contentSections.mechanism: **An explicit ARIA role overrides the computed native role, even when that override actively removes correct semantics.** This is what makes role="presentation" genuinely dangerous to copy-paste: it's not a visual change (sighted users see the identical table) and not a keyboard change (Tab still works exactly as before) — it's purely an accessibility-tree change, which means it's invisible to every kind of testing except an actual screen reader pass or a devtools accessibility-tree inspection.

contentSections.body: This is the origin of ARIA's own first rule, stated plainly in the WAI-ARIA specification itself: if a native HTML element already has the semantics you need, use that instead of re-purposing something else with ARIA. A closely related second rule follows from it: don't change an element's native semantics unless there's a real, specific reason to.

role="presentation" is correct for a genuine layout table and actively destructive on real data — and because it changes nothing visual or keyboard-related, it's one of the easiest defects in this module to ship without noticing.

contentSections.title: ARIA that's wrong isn't neutral — it's worse than none

contentSections.body: A modal's close control visibly says "Cancel." Its markup carries `aria-label="Close"`. A sighted user reads "Cancel." A screen reader user hears "Close" — two different instructions for the exact same control, depending on which sense you're using to operate it.

contentSections.question: What's actually wrong here?

options.label: aria-label overrides the visible text entirely for a screen reader user, so they hear a different, contradictory instruction than what's on screen — worse than having no aria-label at all
Nothing — aria-label is just a redundant backup label
aria-label isn't valid on a <button> element

feedback.contradiction: Right. aria-label sits above visible text content in the accessible-name priority order, so it fully replaces "Cancel" for a screen reader user rather than supplementing it — they hear "Close" and act on that, while a sighted colleague on the same call reads "Cancel" and acts on a subtly different mental model of what the button does.
feedback.redundant: It isn't redundant — it's a full override, not a backup. A screen reader user never hears "Cancel" at all once aria-label is present.
feedback.invalid: aria-label is valid on virtually any element, buttons included — the problem here isn't where it's placed, it's what it says.

contentSections.flawExplanation: "No ARIA is better than bad ARIA" is the operating principle here: a button with no aria-label at all would announce its correct visible text, "Cancel," through the normal text-content fallback. Adding an aria-label that contradicts the visible text doesn't add information, it replaces correct information with wrong information — and a completely unlabeled control at least prompts a careful reviewer to investigate further, where confidently wrong ARIA gives false confidence that the control is fine.

contentSections.body: This specific mismatch — visible text and aria-label saying two different things — is worth actively hunting for in a real audit, because it's invisible to a sighted-only review (the screen looks completely correct) and invisible to most automated scanners (an aria-label is present and non-empty, which is all most tools check). It surfaces only by actually listening to what gets announced and comparing it, word for word, to what's on screen.
ARIA that contradicts what's visibly on screen isn't a lesser version of correct ARIA — it actively misleads a screen reader user, which makes it worse than adding nothing at all.

title: Inspecting the tree in browser devtools
description: Chrome and Firefox both expose the full computed accessibility tree directly in devtools — the fastest way to verify a name/role/value fix without opening a screen reader at all.

learningObjectives.text: Open and read the accessibility tree panel in Chrome or Firefox devtools
Use the computed name/role/properties panel to verify a fix
Build a habit of checking the accessibility tree before reaching for a screen reader

contentSections.title: Where the tree actually lives in devtools

contentSections.body: A developer fixes a labeling bug and wants to confirm it worked. Instead of launching NVDA for a thirty-second spot check, they open Chrome devtools' Elements panel, click the Accessibility tab, and see the exact computed name, role and state for the selected element — no screen reader required.

contentSections.question: Do you need a screen reader running to verify a basic name/role/value fix?
contentSections.answer: Not for a first check. Chrome and Firefox devtools both expose a full accessibility tree inspector — Elements panel → Accessibility tab in Chrome, the Accessibility panel in Firefox — showing computed role, name and state for any selected element, with no screen reader running. It's not a substitute for an actual screen reader pass before shipping (arrow-key behavior inside a widget, announcement timing, live regions in practice only show up with the real tool), but it's the fastest way to verify a specific fix during development.
contentSections.hint: Think about what devtools already show you for CSS — a computed-styles panel that resolves the cascade down to the actual applied value. Is there an equivalent for accessibility properties?

contentSections.body: In Chrome: select an element in the Elements panel, open the Accessibility tab in the sidebar, and it shows Computed Properties — Name, Role, and a full list of exposed ARIA attributes — plus an "Ignored" indicator when an element is excluded from the tree entirely, along with the specific reason (this is exactly where an unexpected `aria-hidden` or `display: none` surprise gets diagnosed fast). Firefox's Accessibility panel does the same job with a slightly different layout, including a checker that flags some common contrast and labeling issues directly in the tree view.
The accessibility tree isn't hidden — it's one click away in devtools, showing exactly what a screen reader would compute, without needing one running.

contentSections.title: Using the tree to verify a fix before ever opening a screen reader

contentSections.body: Back to the disconnected-label bug from earlier in this module. Instead of assuming the fix worked because the markup now looks right, verify it directly in the accessibility tree panel — the same way you'd never ship a CSS fix without actually checking computed styles.

contentSections.question: Put these in order to verify a label fix in devtools.
steps: Select the input element in the Elements panel
Open the Accessibility tab or panel
Check the computed Name field — does it show the expected label text, or is it blank?
If blank, check the Ignored reason and the ARIA attribute list to see what's actually being read instead
Fix the association in the source (for/id, nesting, or aria-labelledby)
Reselect the element and confirm Name now shows the expected text
contentSections.explanation: This is the same discipline as verifying a CSS fix against computed styles rather than trusting the source you just edited: select, inspect the computed value, and only trust the fix once the panel — not your memory of what you just typed — shows the corrected result. Skipping the reselect-and-confirm step is a real, common way a fix that looks right in the diff turns out not to have actually taken effect, because of specificity, load order, or a typo in an id.

contentSections.body: This habit — check the accessibility tree in devtools before, and immediately after, any markup change touching labeling, roles or ARIA state — catches the overwhelming majority of name/role/value defects in seconds, well before a full screen reader pass is needed at all. A screen reader pass still matters for everything devtools can't show (timing, live-region behavior, arrow-key navigation inside a widget), which is exactly why this module builds both skills rather than treating either as sufficient alone.
Check the computed accessibility tree the same way you'd check computed CSS — before trusting that a fix actually took effect, not after.

learningObjectives.text: Predict a control's computed name, role and value from its markup alone
Distinguish which of name, role or value is missing or wrong in a broken snippet

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting if that works, or three — the set doesn't expire and nothing is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Audit a Component Library's Accessibility Tree
description: Pick a real, reused component library and go through it control by control in devtools, recording exactly what name, role and value each one actually exposes.

learningObjectives.text: Inspect a set of real components' computed accessibility tree entries
Diagnose which of name, role or value is missing or wrong for each broken component
Write a component-by-component report a developer can act on without further investigation

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Component libraries are reused everywhere, which means one broken button component is a hundred broken buttons in production, not one — this lab is about finding that kind of defect at its source.

contentSections.title: Component library accessibility-tree audit
contentSections.brief: Pick a real, reused component library you can access today — a design system's Storybook, a component gallery page, or just the reusable buttons/inputs/toggles/dropdowns on a real product you can inspect. For each component, select it in devtools and record its computed name, role and value from the Accessibility panel. Where any of the three is missing, wrong, or contradicts what the component visibly is, log it as a finding.
contentSections.deliverable: A component-by-component report: each component's computed name, role and value as actually exposed, every defect named against which of the three is missing or wrong, and a concrete fix for each.

stages.title: Choose the library and set the scope
stages.instructions: Pick a library or page with at least eight distinct interactive components (buttons, links, checkboxes, toggles, a dropdown, a modal trigger, an icon-only button, a custom widget if one exists). List them before you start inspecting anything, so the audit has a fixed scope instead of drifting.
stages.checkpoint: You have a named list of at least eight components you'll inspect, and access to devtools on the page or Storybook they live on.

stages.title: Inspect each component's computed name, role and value
stages.instructions: For each component: select it in the Elements panel, open the Accessibility tab, and record exactly what Name, Role and any relevant state (checked, expanded, selected) actually show. Don't infer from the markup — read the computed panel directly, the same discipline as the devtools lesson. Note anything that's blank, generic ("button" with no name), or contradicts the component's visible label.
stages.checkpoint: Every component on your list has a recorded computed name, role and value, or a note that one is missing.

stages.title: Diagnose each gap to name, role or value
stages.instructions: For every component with a problem, name specifically which of the three is missing or wrong, and why — a leftover aria-label overriding correct visible text, a div with no implicit role, a custom widget missing aria-checked or aria-expanded, role="presentation" misapplied to real content. Where a component is genuinely fine, say so — not every component in a real library is broken, and confirming the working ones is part of an honest audit.
stages.checkpoint: Every finding names which of name/role/value is affected and the specific markup cause.

stages.title: Write the fix for each finding, and self-check
stages.instructions: For each finding, write the concrete fix — not "add ARIA," but the specific attribute or association needed. Order the report by how many places in the product each component is likely reused (a broken base Button component outranks a one-off custom widget). Then run the self-check against the rubric.
stages.checkpoint: Every finding has a specific fix, findings are ordered by reuse impact, and the report would let a developer act without further investigation.

rubric.criterion: Every component's name, role and value were read from the computed accessibility tree, not inferred from markup
rubric.meets: The devtools Accessibility panel was actually opened and checked for each one, not assumed from reading the HTML.

rubric.criterion: Every finding names specifically which of name, role or value is the problem
rubric.meets: No finding says only "this is broken" — each one states which of the three is missing or wrong.

rubric.criterion: Fixes are specific, not generic
rubric.meets: "Add role=\"switch\" and aria-checked" rather than "add ARIA" or "fix accessibility."

rubric.criterion: Findings are ordered by reuse impact, not discovery order
rubric.meets: A defect in a base, widely-reused component is prioritized above a one-off instance, and the report says why.

rubric.criterion: Working components are confirmed, not just skipped
rubric.meets: At least one component is explicitly noted as correctly exposing name, role and value — an honest audit finds both.

contentSections.body: One broken button component multiplied across a whole product is a much bigger finding than one broken button — this lab is where that math becomes visible.

The accessibility tree — a separate structure the browser computes from the DOM plus ARIA and exposes through a platform accessibility API
The rendered pixels, using image recognition

questions.from: This module — Semantics, Roles and the Accessibility Tree

A `
Save
` looks pixel-identical to a real ``. What role does the div expose in the accessibility tree?

options.label: button, because the visible text reads like one
No implicit role at all — divs carry none, regardless of click handlers or text content
link, the default for anything clickable

This is a bug specific to that screen reader
