title: Zoom, reflow and the horizontal scrollbar that shouldn't exist
description: WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow is specific and testable: no scrolling in two dimensions at 400% zoom, with a short, principled list of real exceptions — not a loophole for an unresponsive layout.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow requires at 400% zoom
Test a page at 400% zoom and diagnose what breaks
Distinguish a real reflow failure from a legitimate exception

contentSections.title: 400% zoom is a real, specific requirement

contentSections.body: Someone with low vision sets their browser to 400% zoom to read a checkout page comfortably. Instead of the layout reflowing into a single readable column, they now have to scroll both down and right for every single line — reading one paragraph means a horizontal scroll for every sentence in it.

contentSections.question: What does WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow actually require at 400% zoom (equivalent to a 320px-wide viewport)?
contentSections.answer: Content has to be readable and operable without scrolling in two dimensions at once. Vertical scrolling for a page of content is completely fine — that's normal. What the criterion prohibits is needing to scroll horizontally (or in both directions together) just to read a single column of text, with a short list of specific, principled exceptions.
contentSections.hint: Think about what a sighted user does at 400% zoom on a well-built responsive page versus a badly-built fixed-width one — one still scrolls down normally, the other adds a second scroll axis entirely.

contentSections.body: The standard test: 400% zoom starting from a 1280px-wide viewport lands you at roughly the same effective width as a 320px viewport — about the width of a typical mobile phone screen. If a page requires horizontal scrolling to read a single column of body text at that width, it fails 1.4.10 Reflow (AA). The criterion has a short, deliberate exception list: content that genuinely requires two-dimensional layout to remain meaningful — data tables, maps, diagrams, video players, games — is explicitly exempted, because reflowing those into a single column would destroy the information itself, not just relocate it. Common real causes of a failure here: a container with a hardcoded pixel width (`width: 1200px`) instead of a fluid or `max-width` rule, layout built with fixed-width flex or grid tracks that never collapse, or a component forced into a rigid horizontal arrangement with no narrower-viewport alternative defined at all — none of which require exotic markup to fix, almost always just a missing responsive breakpoint.
1.4.10 Reflow is about a second scroll axis appearing where it shouldn't — vertical scrolling is always fine, horizontal scrolling for ordinary text at 400% zoom almost never is.

contentSections.title: Diagnosing a reflow failure versus a legitimate exception

contentSections.body: A scheduling app has a data table with fifteen columns of shift times across a week. At 400% zoom, it requires horizontal scrolling to see every column. Is this a WCAG violation?

contentSections.scenario: The fifteen-column shift-schedule table, requiring horizontal scroll at 400% zoom.
contentSections.question: Is horizontal scrolling here a WCAG 1.4.10 violation?

options.label: Yes — any horizontal scrolling at 400% zoom fails 1.4.10, no exceptions
No — this is genuinely tabular data where forcing it into one column would lose the actual relationships between rows and columns; data tables are one of the explicit exceptions to reflow
Only if the table has more than ten columns

feedback.allfail: 1.4.10 has a real, principled exception list, and this scenario is squarely inside it — the criterion was never written to force genuinely tabular data into an unreadable single column.
feedback.exception: Right. This is exactly what the data-table exception exists for: reflowing a real, multi-dimensional schedule into one column wouldn't make it more accessible, it would make the row/column relationships (whose shift, which day) impossible to follow at all.
feedback.columncount: There's no column-count threshold anywhere in the criterion — the test is whether the content is genuinely two-dimensional in meaning, not how many columns it happens to have.

contentSections.mechanism: **Reflow's exception list is specific and principled, not a loophole.** Data tables, maps, and content genuinely requiring two-dimensional layout for meaning are exempt because forcing them into one column would actually destroy information, not just relocate it. The real test is never "does this scroll horizontally" alone — it's "does this genuinely need to, to preserve real meaning, or is this just an unresponsive layout wearing the same symptom."

contentSections.body: This exception gets over-claimed constantly in real audits, and it's worth pushing back on hard when it does: a marketing page laid out with CSS Grid that simply wasn't built responsively is not "like a data table" just because someone points at the same exception clause. The genuine test — would reflowing this into one column actually lose information, versus would it just require a different layout — separates a real exception from the single most common way a real reflow failure gets waved off in a real review.

The reflow exception is for content that would lose real meaning in one column — an unresponsive layout that merely looks similar to a data table doesn't qualify, and it's worth saying so directly when someone claims it does.

title: Text spacing overrides and layouts that shatter
description: WCAG 1.4.12 Text Spacing tests a specific, separate need from zoom — more room between lines and letters, at the same font size — and a layout that survives 400% zoom can still fail it completely.

learningObjectives.text: State the WCAG 1.4.12 Text Spacing values and what they test
Diagnose why increased spacing breaks a layout that worked at the original spacing
Recognize clipped or truncated text as a distinct failure from reflow

contentSections.title: The exact values 1.4.12 tests

contentSections.body: A user applies increased line-height and letter-spacing site-wide — through a browser extension or an OS-level accessibility setting — to make text easier to track without losing their place. A card component's title starts overlapping its own container edges, cut off mid-word, the instant the spacing increases.

contentSections.question: WCAG 1.4.12 Text Spacing specifies exact multipliers a page has to tolerate without losing content or functionality. Roughly what are they?
contentSections.answer: Line height to at least 1.5× the font size, spacing after paragraphs to at least 2× the font size, letter spacing to at least 0.12× the font size, and word spacing to at least 0.16× the font size — applied all at once, typically via a bookmarklet or browser extension during testing.
contentSections.hint: This criterion tests spacing specifically, separately from font size — think about what values would meaningfully loosen up cramped text without doubling its size.

contentSections.body: This is a genuinely separate need from the zoom lesson before it: a user might keep the font size exactly the same and still need more room between lines and letters to track text without losing their place — a real, common need for people with dyslexia and for a range of low-vision conditions. "Make everything bigger" (zoom) and "give me more breathing room at the same size" (spacing) are two different accommodations, and a page can pass one comfortably while failing the other completely.
Text spacing tests a different need than zoom does — more room, not bigger text — and a layout that survives 400% zoom cleanly can still shatter under it.

contentSections.title: Diagnosing the shatter

contentSections.body: The card component from the hook has a fixed-height title area that clips text the instant line-height increases beyond what fits in that fixed pixel height — a defect invisible at default spacing and immediate the moment 1.4.12's values are applied.

contentSections.question: What breaks here under a 1.4.12 text-spacing override?

options.label: The fixed height, overflow: hidden and nowrap together clip the title the instant line-height or letter-spacing grows beyond what fits inside that rigid 24px box
Nothing — height: 24px is only a minimum, so the box will grow as needed
overflow: hidden only affects images, not text

feedback.clipping: Right. `height` (unlike `min-height`) is a hard cap — combined with `overflow: hidden` and `white-space: nowrap`, any increase in line-height or letter-spacing has nowhere to go and gets clipped or cut off mid-word, exactly the failure from the hook.
feedback.minheight: `height` is a fixed, rigid value — it's `min-height` that would let a box grow to fit its content. This is exactly the one-word difference that separates a component that survives spacing overrides from one that shatters under them.
feedback.imagesonly: overflow: hidden clips any overflowing content inside its box, text included — it's one of the most common real causes of text-spacing failures precisely because it's applied constantly, often for unrelated reasons like rounding a card's corners cleanly.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The combination of a fixed pixel height, hidden overflow, and no-wrap text is a pattern that looks completely fine at default spacing and fails immediately once any of the four 1.4.12 values are applied — because the box was never built to accommodate more room than it currently uses, only exactly what it currently uses.

contentSections.body: The fix pattern is consistent: use `min-height` instead of `height` wherever text lives, avoid `white-space: nowrap` on anything user-facing that could legitimately need to wrap, and let containers grow with their content instead of clipping it. None of this requires a visual redesign — it requires the container's CSS to describe a floor, not a fixed size.
A fixed height plus hidden overflow is invisible at default spacing and guaranteed to clip text under a 1.4.12 override — `min-height` instead of `height` is usually the entire fix.

title: Contrast: measuring it, and the cases the ratio misses
description: Three separate contrast thresholds cover text and UI components — and a pair of colors that individually clear every ratio can still fail a colorblind user completely, because contrast and use-of-color are two different criteria.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the correct contrast threshold for normal text, large text, and non-text UI components
Identify what counts as large text under WCAG's own definition
Diagnose a case where passing contrast ratios still fail a real user

contentSections.title: The actual thresholds, and what counts as "large" text

contentSections.body: A designer reports proudly: "everything passes 4.5:1." A large hero heading measured at 3.2:1 still gets flagged during manual review — surprising, since 3.2 sounds like a clear miss of 4.5, not a wrongly-claimed pass.

contentSections.scenario: A page heading is set at 24px, regular weight (not bold).
contentSections.question: Does this heading get evaluated against the 4.5:1 normal-text threshold, or the 3:1 large-text threshold?

options.label: 3:1 — 24px (18pt) regular weight meets WCAG's own definition of large text
4.5:1 — only bold text ever counts as large, regardless of size
7:1 — headings always require AAA-level contrast

feedback.large: Right. WCAG defines large text as at least 18pt (roughly 24px) at regular weight, or at least 14pt (roughly 18.66px) at bold weight — either condition qualifies. This heading meets the size threshold at regular weight, so it gets the relaxed 3:1 requirement, and 3.2:1 genuinely clears it.
feedback.normal: Size alone is enough to qualify — bold isn't required if the text is large enough on its own. This heading's 3.2:1 is actually a pass, not a fail, once the correct threshold is applied.
feedback.aaa: Headings don't automatically require AAA-level contrast — 7:1 is the AAA threshold for normal text specifically, and most real compliance targets (from the earlier phase's law module) sit at AA, not AAA.

contentSections.concept: **"Large text" is a specific, defined size/weight threshold, not a subjective judgment.** At least 18pt (~24px) regular, or at least 14pt (~18.66px) bold, gets the relaxed 3:1 AA threshold instead of 4.5:1, because larger, bolder strokes stay legible at lower contrast. Below that size and weight, it's normal text at 4.5:1. Non-text UI components — icons, input borders, a focus indicator — get their own separate 3:1 requirement under 1.4.11, a completely different criterion from either text threshold.

contentSections.body: Three thresholds worth keeping straight, because mixing them up produces exactly the false alarm from the hook: normal text 4.5:1 (AA), large text 3:1 (AA), non-text UI components and graphical objects 3:1 (1.4.11). None of these apply to logos or purely decorative text — WCAG's own exception — and none apply to a genuinely disabled or inactive control.
"Large text" is a defined size-and-weight threshold with its own relaxed ratio — a passing measurement isn't wrong just because the number looks lower than the 4.5:1 most people remember by default.

contentSections.title: Where a passing ratio still isn't the whole story

contentSections.body: A status list uses green text for "Active" and red text for "Inactive," each individually clearing 4.5:1 against the white background behind it. For a colorblind user, the two colors read as nearly identical — and there's no icon, label or shape distinguishing one from the other.

contentSections.scenario: Green #1a7a1a and red #c0392b text, both individually passing 4.5:1 against a white background, used as the only distinguisher between "Active" and "Inactive."
contentSections.question: Both colors pass the contrast ratio individually. What's the actual accessibility gap here?

options.label: Color is the only thing distinguishing the two states — WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color requires a non-color distinguisher in addition to color, and a contrast ratio measurement says nothing about this at all
Nothing is missing — both ratios pass, so this is fully compliant
The red specifically needs a higher ratio than the green to compensate

feedback.useofcolor: Right. Contrast ratio (1.4.3/1.4.11) and use of color (1.4.1) are two completely separate criteria testing two different things — one measures how visible a color is against its background, the other requires that meaning never depends on color alone. Passing the first says nothing whatsoever about the second.
feedback.nothingmissing: Both ratios passing is real and good — but it answers a different question than the one this scenario is actually raising, which is whether a colorblind user (or someone viewing a black-and-white printout, or reading in bright glare) can tell the two states apart at all.
feedback.asymmetric: Contrast ratios aren't compared against each other this way — each color's ratio against the background is independent, and neither needing a "higher" ratio would fix the actual gap, which is the total absence of any non-color distinguisher.

contentSections.mechanism: **Contrast ratio and use-of-color are two separate, independently-testable requirements, and a page can pass one while failing the other completely.** A color-blind user, someone viewing a black-and-white printout, or someone reading in bright sunlight glare may not distinguish red from green at all, regardless of how cleanly each one individually measures against the background — which is exactly why the fix here is adding an icon, a label, or a pattern, never a different shade of red or green.

contentSections.body: The same caution from the keyboard module's focus-ring lesson applies here too: a single-point contrast checker sampling a photographic or gradient background can mislead in either direction, reporting a pass or fail that doesn't hold everywhere the text actually sits — worth spot-checking the worst-looking region by eye, not trusting one automated sample.
A passing contrast ratio says nothing about whether color alone is carrying meaning — those are two separate criteria, and real findings need both checked independently.

title: Using a magnifier: context loss and the off-screen change
description: A screen magnifier shows a small, panned window over a much larger virtual canvas — and dynamic content that appears outside that window might as well not exist, unless something actively moves the window there.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what a screen magnifier actually shows versus a full page
Diagnose a defect caused by content changing outside the magnified viewport
Recommend where dynamic feedback needs to appear for a magnifier user to see it

contentSections.title: A magnifier shows a window, not a page

contentSections.body: A reviewer turns on a screen magnifier at 300% and discovers the real experience is nothing like "big text." It's a small, moving window panning across a much larger virtual canvas, and most of the actual page is permanently off-screen at any given moment.

contentSections.question: A sighted user glances at a whole 1920px-wide page at once. What does a 300% magnifier user see at any given moment?
contentSections.answer: Roughly a third of that width at a time — a small, panned viewport moving over a much larger virtual canvas, tracking either the mouse pointer, the current keyboard focus, or the text cursor depending on the tool's settings. Context a sighted user gets for free just by glancing at the whole screen — where they are on the page, what else is nearby — has to be actively rebuilt through panning, one small window at a time.
contentSections.hint: Screen magnification doesn't shrink the page to fit a bigger view — it enlarges a portion of it and moves what's actually visible around.

contentSections.body: Magnifiers offer different tracking modes, and which one is active changes what a reviewer actually needs to test: follow-mouse, follow-keyboard-focus, and follow-text-cursor are all common. A reviewer testing a keyboard-driven flow specifically should switch to focus-tracking mode, since that's the closest match to how a magnifier user actually navigates a form or a multi-step process without a mouse.
A magnifier doesn't show a bigger page — it shows a small window onto a much bigger one, and everything outside that window is, for the moment, effectively gone.

contentSections.title: When something changes where the magnified window isn't

contentSections.body: A long form's validation error appears above the submit button, at the very top of the page. A magnifier user, zoomed in on the submit button they just clicked near the bottom, never pans up far enough to see it — from where they're looking, the form appears to have simply done nothing at all.

contentSections.problem: Diagnose why the form "seems to silently do nothing" for a magnifier user, even though it's actually showing a validation error.

steps.label: Confirm the error genuinely renders
steps.work: The error message is present in the DOM and visible on screen — this is a real, rendered element, not a screen-reader-only gap.
steps.why: Ruling out "it doesn't exist" narrows the problem to specifically where it exists relative to what's currently visible.

steps.label: Check where it renders relative to the current viewport
steps.work: The error appears at the top of a long form; the magnifier's panned window is still centred on the submit button near the bottom.
steps.why: This is the actual mechanism — the content and the visible window are simply in different places.

steps.label: Identify the real cause
steps.work: Nothing about the page draws the magnified viewport toward the error's location — no focus move, no scroll, nothing.
steps.why: A defect only becomes fixable once you can name what specifically should have happened and didn't.

steps.label: State what's needed
steps.work: Move keyboard focus to the error message (or to the first invalid field) on submission, so a focus-tracking magnifier follows it there automatically.
steps.why: This is the exact same mechanism that helps a screen reader user, from the previous module's live-region and focus-move lessons — one fix serves both.

steps.label: Name what this costs the user right now
steps.work: A magnifier user reasonably assumes their click did nothing, and may resubmit repeatedly or abandon the form entirely.
steps.why: Naming the concrete real-world consequence, not just "error not visible," is what makes this finding land as urgent rather than cosmetic.

faded.problem: A second case: a toast notification appears in a corner of the screen and auto-dismisses after three seconds, far from wherever the magnifier's viewport currently happens to be.

blanks.prompt: What happens to a magnifier user who never pans there in time? (describe in a few words)
blanks.answer: they never see it at all
accept: it disappears before they see it
the message is gone before they can find it
blanks.why: A toast that self-dismisses gives a magnifier user no cue to look for it and no time to pan there even if they somehow knew to — the timing itself is the second half of the defect, on top of the location.

blanks.prompt: What single mechanism would fix both this case and the form-error case above?
blanks.why: Moving focus is the one intervention that reaches a screen reader user, a keyboard user, and a focus-tracking magnifier user simultaneously — exactly why it recurs across every module in this phase rather than being a magnifier-specific trick.

contentSections.procedure: **Dynamic feedback has to reach wherever the magnified viewport actually is, not wherever a sighted, non-magnified user's eyes would naturally land.** Moving focus is the single mechanism that serves a screen reader user, a keyboard user, and a focus-tracking magnifier user all at once — which is exactly why it keeps reappearing as the fix across this whole phase, not a coincidence.

contentSections.body: Content that changes outside a magnifier's current viewport might as well not exist, until something actively moves the viewport there — and moving focus is the one fix that does that for every assistive technology at once.

title: High contrast and forced colours modes
description: Forced-colours mode is a real, user-controlled OS feature that strips a page's author-chosen palette down to a small system set — and any component relying on background-color alone to show its state disappears under it.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what OS-level forced-colours mode actually does to a page's CSS
Diagnose a component that becomes unusable specifically under forced colours
Recognize where CSS decisions commonly break under forced colours

contentSections.title: What forced colours actually strips out

contentSections.body: A reviewer turns on Windows High Contrast mode — forced colours, in CSS terms — and a whole product's carefully designed palette vanishes, replaced by a small, strict system palette the OS enforces. Several buttons that relied purely on background-color to look like buttons become invisible outlines with no fill at all.

contentSections.question: What does forced-colours mode actually do to a page's CSS?
contentSections.answer: The OS overrides most author-specified colors — background-color, color, border-color and more — with a small, fixed system palette the user has chosen, usually for contrast or light-sensitivity reasons, while leaving layout, spacing and non-color styling untouched. Background images are typically stripped entirely too, unless a page explicitly opts back in for a specific element.
contentSections.hint: This is a real accessibility feature someone deliberately turns on, not a rendering glitch — think about what it would need to preserve (readability, high contrast) versus what it would happily discard (a brand's specific color choices).

contentSections.body: This is a user-controlled accessibility setting, not a bug in the browser or the OS — someone with low vision or light sensitivity turns it on deliberately, for real, specific reasons. A page that becomes unusable under it is failing an accessibility feature the operating system itself provides, which makes it a squarely testable, real-world scenario in an audit, not an edge case to wave off as unlikely.
Forced-colours mode is a deliberate, user-chosen accessibility setting — a component that breaks under it is failing a real feature real users turn on, not an unusual edge case.

contentSections.title: Where components typically break

contentSections.body: A custom checkbox is styled entirely with background-color: checked state is a filled blue square, unchecked is an empty square, with no border and no icon anywhere. Under forced colours, both states become identical empty squares — the only thing distinguishing them was exactly the property the OS overrides.

contentSections.question: What breaks under forced-colours mode?

options.label: background-color is exactly what forced-colours strips out, and with no border or icon as a fallback distinguisher, checked and unchecked become visually identical
Nothing — forced colours only affects text color, not backgrounds
The checkbox becomes unclickable under forced colours

feedback.identical: Right. The only visual distinguisher between the two states was a background-color change, and that's precisely the property forced-colours overrides. With no border, icon or other non-color signal built in as a fallback, both states collapse into the same empty square.
feedback.textonly: Forced-colours affects background-color, border-color and more, not just text — this checkbox's entire state-indicator relied on exactly the property that gets overridden.
feedback.unclickable: Click behavior is untouched — this is purely a visual defect. The checkbox still toggles when clicked; a user simply can no longer tell which state it's currently in.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A control whose entire visual state depends on a single color property, with nothing else backing it up, is a defect waiting for exactly this trigger — it costs nothing under normal rendering and fails completely the moment the OS enforces its own palette.

contentSections.body: The fix pattern: use the `forced-colors` CSS media feature to provide an explicit fallback — a visible border, an SVG checkmark drawn with `currentColor` or one of the forced-colors system keywords (`Highlight`, `ButtonText`) — so state is communicated through something other than a background fill alone. This is the same "don't rely on color alone" principle from the contrast lesson, just triggered by a different mechanism: forced-colors mode instead of color blindness, with the same underlying fix either way.
Any control whose entire state depends on background-color alone is one forced-colours activation away from becoming indistinguishable — a border, icon, or other non-color signal is what survives it.

title: Practice — Test Eight Layouts at 400% and Record the Failures
description: Eight drills across the module's skills. No new concepts: this is where recognising a zoom, spacing, contrast or forced-colours failure stops being something you've read about.

learningObjectives.text: Apply reflow, text-spacing, contrast and forced-colours diagnosis to unfamiliar scenarios at speed
Distinguish a real low-vision failure from a legitimate exception or a false alarm

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Eight drills across the module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Do them in one sitting if that works, or three — the set doesn't expire and nothing is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's the thing to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Run a Full Low-Vision Pass on a Real Product
description: One product, five separate low-vision checks — zoom and reflow, text spacing, contrast, a magnifier pass, and forced colours — each producing its own findings.

learningObjectives.text: Test a real product across zoom, reflow, text spacing, contrast and forced colours
Diagnose each failure to its specific CSS or design cause
Distinguish real failures from legitimate exceptions across all five checks

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Five separate lenses on the same product, one after another — each one finds things the others wouldn't, which is exactly why a real low-vision pass isn't just "zoom in and look around."

contentSections.title: Full low-vision pass
contentSections.brief: Pick a real product or a few key flows within one. Run five checks in sequence: 400% zoom/reflow, a text-spacing override (bookmarklet or extension), contrast measurement on your most-used text and UI components, a screen-magnifier pass at 300%, and forced-colours mode. Log every genuine failure, and just as importantly, note where something looked broken at first glance but turned out to be a legitimate exception once you checked it properly.
contentSections.deliverable: A pass report organized into five sections — zoom/reflow, text spacing, contrast, magnifier, forced colours — each with its findings, their location, and a fix.

stages.title: Zoom, reflow and text spacing
stages.instructions: Set browser zoom to 400% and check for horizontal scrolling on ordinary content (not tables, maps or similarly exempt content). Then apply a text-spacing override (line-height 1.5×, paragraph spacing 2×, letter-spacing 0.12×, word-spacing 0.16×) via a bookmarklet or extension, and look for clipped, overlapping, or truncated text. Log every real failure with its location.
stages.checkpoint: You have findings (or a confirmed clean pass) for both zoom/reflow and text-spacing overrides, with any exceptions specifically justified, not just noted as "probably fine."

stages.title: Contrast: text and non-text
stages.instructions: Measure contrast on your most-used body text, your largest headings, and at least three non-text UI components (icons, input borders, a focus indicator) using a contrast checker. Apply the correct threshold to each — 4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text, 3:1 non-text components — and separately check whether any status or meaning relies on color alone with no other distinguisher.
stages.checkpoint: Every measured element has its correct threshold applied, and use-of-color is checked as a separate question from contrast ratio.

stages.title: Magnifier pass
stages.instructions: Turn on a screen magnifier at 300%, in focus-tracking mode if available. Complete a real task (a form, a multi-step flow) using only what's visible in the magnified viewport at each step. Note anywhere dynamic content — an error, a confirmation, a status change — appeared outside the current viewport with nothing drawing you there.
stages.checkpoint: You've completed a real task under magnification and logged every point where off-screen content would have gone unnoticed.

stages.title: Forced colours, and self-check
stages.instructions: Turn on forced-colours/high-contrast mode and check every custom component whose state depends on color — checkboxes, toggles, selected/unselected states, status indicators. Log anything that becomes indistinguishable. Then run the self-check against the rubric below before calling this done.
stages.checkpoint: Every color-dependent component has been checked under forced colours, and the full five-section report is ready for self-check.

rubric.criterion: All five checks were actually run, not assumed from earlier findings
rubric.meets: Zoom/reflow, text spacing, contrast, magnifier and forced colours each have their own section with real findings or a confirmed clean pass.

rubric.criterion: Exceptions are justified, not just claimed
rubric.meets: Anywhere a finding is dismissed as an exception (a data table, a decorative element), the report states specifically why it qualifies.

rubric.criterion: Use-of-color is checked separately from contrast ratio
rubric.meets: At least one finding (or confirmed pass) specifically addresses whether meaning depends on color alone, distinct from any ratio measurement.

rubric.criterion: The magnifier pass actually completed a real task
rubric.meets: Not just a visual scan — an actual multi-step task was attempted and completed (or blocked) using only the magnified viewport.

rubric.criterion: Every finding names a specific, fixable cause
rubric.meets: A finding says what CSS property or design decision caused it, not just that something "looks broken."

contentSections.body: Five different lenses on the same product surface five genuinely different classes of defect — running only one of them is how a real low-vision audit ends up calling a product accessible when it's only accessible along the one axis someone happened to check.

title: Checkpoint — Magnification, Zoom and Low Vision
description: Ten questions pulling across this module, the semantics module before it, and two modules further back. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Magnification, Zoom and Low Vision

questions.from: This module — Magnification, Zoom and Low Vision
questions.prompt: A page requires horizontal scrolling to read a single column of ordinary text at 400% zoom. What does this fail?

options.label: WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow — normal content shouldn't need two-dimensional scrolling at that zoom level
Nothing — horizontal scrolling is always acceptable at high zoom levels
WCAG 1.4.3 Contrast, since zoom and contrast are the same requirement

questions.explanation: 1.4.10 Reflow specifically prohibits needing to scroll in two dimensions for ordinary content at 400% zoom — vertical scrolling is fine, this added horizontal axis is the actual failure.

questions.from: This module — Magnification, Zoom and Low Vision
questions.prompt: A 15-column data table requires horizontal scrolling at 400% zoom. Is this a reflow violation?

options.label: No — genuinely tabular data is one of reflow's explicit, principled exceptions, since forcing it into one column would destroy the actual relationships
Yes, always — tables are never exempt
Only if it has more than 20 columns

questions.explanation: Data tables are one of the specific, principled exceptions — the test is whether reflowing would genuinely lose meaning, not the column count.

questions.from: This module — Magnification, Zoom and Low Vision
questions.prompt: Two status colors (green "Active," red "Inactive") both individually pass 4.5:1 contrast against their background. Is that sufficient for accessibility?

options.label: No — color is the only distinguisher between the two states, and WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color requires a non-color signal too, independent of contrast ratio
Yes — passing contrast is the only requirement that applies here
No — the ratios need to be higher, at least 7:1 each

questions.explanation: Contrast ratio and use of color are separate criteria — a colorblind user may not distinguish red from green regardless of how well each individually measures against the background.

questions.from: This module — Magnification, Zoom and Low Vision
questions.prompt: A checkbox's checked state is shown purely with a background-color fill, no border or icon. What happens under forced-colours mode?

options.label: Checked and unchecked become visually identical, since background-color is exactly what the OS overrides
Nothing changes — forced colours only affects text
The checkbox stops being clickable

questions.explanation: background-color is precisely the property forced-colours mode overrides — with no border or icon as a fallback, the only signal distinguishing the two states disappears.

questions.from: Previous module — Semantics, Roles and the Accessibility Tree
questions.prompt: A div with an onclick handler and visible text reading "Save" — what role does it expose in the accessibility tree?

options.label: button, because the visible text reads like one
No implicit role at all — divs carry none, regardless of click handlers or text content
link, the default for anything clickable

questions.explanation: A div carries no implicit role under any circumstance — role comes only from the actual element or an explicit ARIA role, never from behavior or text content.

questions.from: Previous module — Semantics, Roles and the Accessibility Tree
questions.prompt: A field has both a correctly connected native label AND a leftover aria-label with different, older text. Which wins the accessible name?

options.label: The native label, since it's programmatically correct
The aria-label — it sits higher in the accessible-name priority order and fully overrides native labeling
Whichever appears first in the HTML source

questions.explanation: aria-label wins outright, even over a fully correct native label — exactly how a stale attribute can silently defeat a properly connected label added later.

questions.from: Previous module — Semantics, Roles and the Accessibility Tree
questions.prompt: role="presentation" applied to a real financial data table with genuine headers. What does a screen reader user lose?

options.label: Header, row and column announcement and navigation — the table announces as generic content instead of tabular data
Nothing — role=presentation only affects visual styling
Keyboard access to the table's cells

questions.explanation: role="presentation" strips exactly the row/column/header relationships table-navigation commands depend on — purely an accessibility-tree change, invisible to sighted testing.

questions.from: Older module — Keyboard-Only Operation
questions.prompt: What contrast ratio must a focus indicator itself meet against its adjacent colours, per WCAG 1.4.11?

options.label: 7:1, the same as AAA text contrast

title: Switch scanning: every extra control costs real time
description: A switch user isn't pointing at anything — a highlight moves through the page's controls on a timer, and every extra control between the start and the one they want adds real, mechanical time to every single action.

learningObjectives.text: Explain how switch scanning works and why control count directly costs time
Estimate how long a given control takes to reach under linear scanning
Identify what actually reduces switch-scanning time versus what's cosmetic

contentSections.title: One or two buttons, and a moving highlight

contentSections.body: A switch user with limited mobility operates a computer with a single button — a puff-switch, a head-switch, sometimes just one working finger on one key. The screen highlights each interactive element in turn, one at a time, on a timer. Pressing the switch at the right moment selects whatever's currently highlighted. There's no pointing, no typing shortcuts — just waiting for the highlight to reach the right thing, then acting.

contentSections.question: If a page has 40 interactive elements and a linear scanner highlights one at a time, roughly a second apart, how long could it take to reach the 35th one?
contentSections.answer: Potentially over thirty seconds for a single action, if the target sits near the end of the scan order. Every extra control between the start of the scan and the one a user actually wants adds real, mechanical time — unlike a mouse click, which costs the same fraction of a second regardless of how many other things happen to be on the page.
contentSections.hint: A mouse user's cost to click something doesn't scale with how many other buttons are nearby. Does a switch user's cost work the same way?

contentSections.body: Real switch-access software (Switch Control on iOS and macOS, Android's own Switch Access) offers two main scanning patterns. **Linear scanning** highlights every element in order, one at a time — simple, but the worst case scales directly with total control count. **Row-column scanning** groups elements (usually visually, into rows), scans across the groups first, then scans within whichever group is selected — dramatically faster for a page with many controls, but only works well when the underlying markup actually has recognizable groups (headings, fieldsets, landmarks) for the software to organize by. A user can adjust scan speed and pattern, but the OS can't invent structure a page never provided.
Switch scanning cost isn't abstract — it's roughly proportional to how many controls sit between the start of the scan and the one a user actually wants.

contentSections.title: What actually reduces scan time

contentSections.body: A smart-home app's settings page lists sixty individual device toggles in one flat sequence, with no grouping by room, category, or anything else — just sixty items, one after another, in whatever order they happen to render.

contentSections.problem: Diagnose why this page is nearly unusable for a switch user, and what a real fix requires.

steps.label: Confirm the current cost
steps.work: Switch access has to step through up to sixty highlight-stops in linear order to reach the last toggle.
steps.why: This isn't a crash or a broken control — it's a structural cost that scales purely with how many items exist in the scan sequence.

steps.label: Identify what real grouping would need
steps.work: Row-column scanning needs recognizable regions — fieldsets with a legend, headings, ARIA groups — that the software can present as a first-level choice before scanning within one.
steps.why: This is the same structural markup (headings, landmarks, grouping) that helps a screen reader user, doing a genuinely different job here — cutting mechanical scan time rather than aiding orientation.

steps.label: State the fix
steps.work: Group the sixty toggles under headings or fieldsets by room or category, so scanning steps through a handful of groups first, then individual toggles only within the one selected.
steps.why: This turns a worst case of sixty sequential steps into roughly (number of groups) + (toggles in one group) — often a tenth of the original cost for a toggle near the end.

steps.label: Name the cost of leaving it unfixed
steps.work: For the fifty-fifth toggle, this is a fixed cost of fifty-five highlight-steps, every single time, for as long as the flat structure exists.
steps.why: Naming the concrete, recurring cost — not just "hard to use" — is what makes this finding land as a real priority rather than a nice-to-have.

faded.problem: A second question about the same page: does removing a decorative, non-functional logo link (one that doesn't actually go anywhere) from the scan order help?

blanks.prompt: Would removing a pointless-but-focusable element from the scan sequence help a switch user? (yes or no)
blanks.why: Every focusable-but-non-operative element the scan visits is pure lost time — it's never useful to a switch user and always costs a highlight-step.

blanks.prompt: What general principle does this point at, beyond this one logo link?
blanks.answer: minimize what's focusable to what's actually operable and useful
blanks.why: The number of genuinely focusable elements on a page is itself a switch-access design decision, not just a keyboard-navigation one — trimming decorative or redundant focusable elements measurably helps.

contentSections.procedure: **Switch scanning cost is roughly proportional to control count, and it's directly improved by real grouping.** The same structural elements — headings, landmarks, fieldsets — that help a screen reader user orient also directly cut a switch user's wait time, for a mechanically different reason: one is about finding meaning faster, the other is about a literal, ticking clock on every single action.

contentSections.body: A flat page with sixty controls costs a switch user roughly sixty steps for the last one — real grouping (headings, fieldsets, landmarks) is what turns that into a handful.

title: Target size, spacing and motor precision
description: 24 CSS pixels isn't an arbitrary number — it's the specific, measurable line between a target someone with a tremor or limited fine motor control can hit reliably and one they can't.

learningObjectives.text: State the WCAG 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) requirement and its exceptions
Diagnose why closely-spaced small targets cost more than they visually appear to
Measure a target's actual size directly in devtools

contentSections.title: The actual number, and why it isn't arbitrary

contentSections.body: A delivery app's "increase quantity" and "remove item" buttons sit four pixels apart, each about 20 by 20 pixels. For a precise mouse user, that's fine. For someone with a tremor or limited fine motor control, that four-pixel gap is the difference between adjusting a quantity and accidentally deleting the item entirely.

contentSections.question: WCAG 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) sets a specific minimum size for pointer targets. What is it?
contentSections.answer: 24 by 24 CSS pixels (AA), unless a specific exception applies — inline text links within a paragraph, a target that's already the smallest of several equivalent controls where a larger version of the same action is available nearby, or spacing between targets that compensates for a smaller size.
contentSections.hint: This is a real, measurable pixel dimension, not a vague "make it bigger" guideline — think about what number would matter for a fingertip on a touchscreen, not just a mouse cursor.

contentSections.body: The spacing exception is worth understanding precisely, because it's the one most often invoked (correctly or not) in a real review: a target smaller than 24px can still pass if there's enough surrounding space that a 24px circle centered on it wouldn't overlap the equivalent circle around the next target. Size and spacing genuinely trade off against each other — a smaller target with generous space around it can meet the criterion, and a 24px target crammed against its neighbor with zero gap might still cause real mis-taps in practice even where it technically passes.
24 by 24 CSS pixels is the specific number, and size trades off against spacing — not a size someone eyeballs as "probably fine."

contentSections.title: Why this matters beyond switch and voice users specifically

contentSections.body: This module's throughline shows up again here: someone with a tremor, someone using a touchscreen on a moving bus, someone with a temporary injury like a broken hand — none of them are specifically "switch users," and all of them hit the exact same small-target problem.

contentSections.scenario: A table row has two icon-only buttons, "Edit" (pencil) and "Delete" (trash), each 18 by 18 pixels, placed with zero gap between them.
contentSections.question: Does this meet WCAG 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)?

options.label: No — each target is under 24px and there's no compensating spacing to make up for it
Yes — icon-only buttons are automatically exempt from target size requirements
This criterion only applies to touchscreens, not desktop pointer input

feedback.fails: Right. 18px is under the 24px minimum, and with zero gap between the two buttons there's no spacing compensation either — this fails cleanly, and it's exactly the shape of finding (two destructive-adjacent-to-non-destructive actions, both undersized) worth flagging with real urgency.
feedback.iconexempt: There's no such exemption — "it's an icon" isn't one of the listed exceptions. Size is size, regardless of what's rendered inside the target.
feedback.touchonly: 2.5.8 applies to pointer input generally, not exclusively touchscreens — mouse users with motor impairments benefit from adequately sized, spaced targets too.

contentSections.concept: **The exceptions to 2.5.8 are a short, specific list, and "it's an icon" or "this is desktop, not mobile" aren't on it.** Size is measured the same way regardless of what's visually inside the target or what device class the page happens to be viewed on.

contentSections.body: This is one of the more straightforward WCAG criteria to actually measure in a real review: select the element in devtools, read its rendered box dimensions directly from the computed layout, and check the gap to its nearest neighbor. No interpretation required, unlike a criterion like Focus Order that needs judgment about what "meaningful sequence" even means for a given page.

An 18px delete button with zero gap next to an 18px edit button is both undersized and unspaced — and adjacent to a destructive action, which makes the real-world cost of a mis-tap worse than the number alone suggests.

title: Voice control: you can only click what has a name you can say
description: Voice control software matches spoken commands against the exact same accessible-name computation from the semantics module — a control with no name, or a name shared by five others, becomes unreachable by voice for reasons that have nothing to do with speech recognition.

learningObjectives.text: Explain how voice control matches spoken commands to on-screen controls
Diagnose why a missing or generic accessible name makes a control unreachable by voice
Explain why voice control depends on the same naming work as screen readers, for a different reason

contentSections.title: "Click Submit" only works if something is actually named "Submit"

contentSections.body: A user with a repetitive strain injury operates their computer entirely with voice — Dragon NaturallySpeaking, or the built-in Voice Control on macOS or Windows — saying "click Submit," "click Email," "click Menu" to interact with a page. No mouse, no keyboard, purely speech-driven commands matched against what's on screen.

contentSections.question: How does voice control software actually know what "click Submit" refers to?
contentSections.answer: It reads the accessible name of every clickable or interactive element on the page — the exact same computation from the semantics module — and matches spoken words against those names. If nothing's accessible name is "Submit," there's nothing to click, no matter how obviously a sighted user would recognize a "Submit" button by its visual label alone.
contentSections.hint: Voice software isn't reading pixels or guessing at intent — it needs a concrete, computed piece of text to match your words against. Where would it get that text from?

contentSections.body: Most voice control tools offer a fallback for anything with no usable name: numbered overlay grids ("click 7") that label every clickable element with a visible number, regardless of whether it has a real accessible name. Genuinely useful as a last resort, and a strictly worse experience — it trades a natural, meaningful command ("click Submit") for memorizing or reading a number off an overlay that has to be invoked as an extra step first, on every single page that needs it.

Voice control reads the exact same accessible name a screen reader would — an unnamed control isn't just silent to one assistive technology, it's unreachable to a second one for the same underlying reason.

contentSections.title: Generic and duplicate names are a voice-specific problem too

contentSections.body: A product listing page has six identical "Add to cart" buttons, one per product — the same scenario from the automated-testing-limits module, back in the foundations phase. For a screen reader user, that's mildly disorienting. For a voice control user, saying "click Add to cart" is now genuinely ambiguous.

contentSections.scenario: Six identically-named "Add to cart" buttons; a voice control user says "click Add to cart."
contentSections.question: What actually happens?

options.label: Voice control finds multiple matches and either numbers all six for the user to pick manually, or the command fails as ambiguous — either way, the natural single-word command that works fine on a well-named page simply doesn't work here
Voice control always picks the first match automatically and correctly
Nothing — voice control only matches against unique element IDs, not accessible names, so this is unrelated

feedback.ambiguous: Right. With six identical matches, the tool either falls back to numbering all of them (adding the exact same extra step as the earlier unnamed-control case) or the command simply fails — neither is the fast, natural interaction voice control is supposed to provide.
feedback.autopick: There's no reliable "always the first one" behavior a user could depend on — and even if there were, picking the wrong one of six products silently would be worse than a failed command.
feedback.idsonly: Voice control matches against accessible names specifically, the same computation covered in the semantics module — element IDs generally aren't user-facing text at all and play no part in this matching.

contentSections.mechanism: **Naming quality isn't a one-audience concern — it's foundational infrastructure that multiple, completely different assistive technologies depend on independently.** The screen reader problem with six identical buttons was disorientation; the voice control problem with the same six buttons is genuine ambiguity that breaks the command outright. Same root defect, two different mechanisms of harm, which is exactly why fixing accessible names once pays off across every assistive technology at once rather than needing a separate fix per tool.

contentSections.body: The fix is the same one that would have helped the screen reader user: unique, distinguishing accessible names per product — "Add Wireless Headphones X200 to cart" instead of a bare "Add to cart" repeated six times. Voice control just makes the cost of skipping that fix land differently: not confusion, but an outright broken command.

Six identically-named buttons are a mild finding for a screen reader user and a hard failure for a voice control user — the same defect, landing differently depending on which assistive technology is trying to use the name.

title: Timeouts that assume a fast user
description: A time limit that's comfortable for a mouse user can be mechanically impossible for a switch or voice control user, for reasons that have nothing to do with hesitation — and WCAG 2.2.1 requires a real way to turn it off, extend it, or be warned first.

learningObjectives.text: State what WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable requires for most time limits
Diagnose why a fixed timeout disproportionately affects switch and voice users specifically
Identify the narrow, legitimate exceptions to the timing-adjustable requirement

contentSections.title: A 90-second timeout is a sprint for some users and impossible for others

contentSections.body: A banking site logs a user out after ninety seconds of "inactivity" during a form. For a mouse and keyboard user, that's plenty of time. For a switch user scanning through a ten-field form one highlight-step at a time, ninety seconds might not be enough to complete even the first three fields — and every switch press genuinely is activity, but the site's inactivity timer may only reset on mouse movement or events it was never built to recognize from switch or voice input.

contentSections.question: What does WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable require for most content-imposed time limits?
contentSections.answer: The user must be able to turn the limit off, adjust it (extend it significantly — commonly to at least ten times the default), or be warned and given at least twenty seconds to request more time before it expires. There are narrow, specific exceptions: genuinely real-time events (a live auction), and limits that are essential to the activity itself (a timed test where completing it quickly is literally the thing being measured).
contentSections.hint: Think about the three separate options this criterion actually offers — off, adjustable, or warned-with-a-chance-to-extend — rather than a single fixed rule.

contentSections.body: The "essential" exception is narrow, and it's worth naming plainly how often it gets misapplied in practice: a session timeout justified purely as "security" is almost never actually essential in the WCAG sense. Warning a user and letting them extend the session doesn't meaningfully weaken real security — a silent hard cutoff with no warning is a design choice, not a security requirement, and it's one of the more common places a reviewer needs to push back on "we can't change that, it's for security" with a specific question: what security property would actually break if this became warn-and-extend instead of silent-and-final?

"It's for security" rarely survives the actual essential-exception test — warn-and-extend serves the same security goal as a silent cutoff, without excluding anyone whose input method is inherently slower.

contentSections.title: Why this hits switch and voice users hardest, specifically

contentSections.body: Switch scanning cost scales with control count (this module's first lesson); voice control needs clean, distinguishable spoken commands (the lesson before this one). Both mean a task that takes a mouse user twenty seconds might take a switch or voice user several minutes — for reasons that have nothing to do with hesitation or distraction, purely the mechanical cost of their input method.

contentSections.code: Complete checkout within 5:00
contentSections.question: What's the actual defect here?

options.label: No mechanism to extend, turn off, or get warned before the limit expires — exactly the WCAG 2.2.1 gap, and it disproportionately punishes users whose input method is inherently slower through no fault of their own
Five minutes is generous enough for everyone, so there's no real issue here
This is only a problem if the timer is under sixty seconds

feedback.notiming: Right. Five minutes might genuinely be enough for a mouse user and nowhere near enough for a switch user working through a multi-field checkout one scan-step at a time — the actual defect is the total absence of any adjust/extend/warn mechanism, not the specific number of minutes chosen.
feedback.enoughtime: "Enough for everyone" is exactly the assumption this lesson is built to challenge — a duration that comfortably clears a mouse user's needs can still be mechanically impossible for a switch or voice user, independent of how generous it looks on its face.
feedback.underminute: There's no duration threshold in the criterion at all — a content-imposed time limit needs an adjust/extend/warn mechanism regardless of whether it's set to sixty seconds or five minutes.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A fixed countdown with zero mechanism to interact with it fails 2.2.1 regardless of how long the duration is, because the actual requirement is about giving the user *some* control over the limit — off, adjustable, or warned-with-extension — not about hitting a specific number of minutes that happens to feel generous to whoever set it.

contentSections.body: The fix pattern: warn at least twenty seconds before expiry with a visible, keyboard/switch/voice-operable "extend" control, and default the extension to something generous rather than making a user request more time repeatedly — a switch or voice user who has to re-request an extension every ninety seconds is still being punished by the underlying design, just more slowly.
A time limit that looks generous to whoever set it can still be mechanically impossible for a switch or voice user — the fix is a real adjust/extend/warn mechanism, not a longer fixed number.

title: Drag, hover and gestures with no alternative
description: Drag-only reordering and hover-only reveals both quietly exclude switch and voice control users completely — and hover-only interactions, specifically, usually turn out to fail keyboard users too, for the same underlying reason this whole phase keeps returning to.

learningObjectives.text: State the WCAG requirements for drag operations and content on hover/focus
Diagnose why drag-only and hover-only interactions exclude switch, voice and motor-impaired users
Identify a click-based or tap-based alternative for a common drag/hover pattern

contentSections.title: Drag needs a single-pointer alternative

contentSections.body: A file-manager UI lets users reorder items only by dragging — no "move up"/"move down" buttons, no keyboard reorder shortcut. A switch or voice control user, who cannot perform a continuous drag gesture at all (switch access has no way to represent "hold and move continuously"; voice control's drag emulation is unreliable and slow even where it exists), simply cannot reorder anything.

contentSections.question: What does WCAG 2.5.7 Dragging Movements require for a drag-based interaction?
contentSections.answer: A single-pointer alternative that doesn't require dragging — buttons, a menu option, or any other way to achieve the same result with a simple click, tap, or activation — unless dragging is genuinely essential to the function itself (a freehand drawing tool, where the drag movement is literally the point of the interaction).
contentSections.hint: The criterion doesn't ban drag interactions outright — it requires an alternative path to the same outcome for anyone who can't perform a drag gesture.

contentSections.body: This is a relatively recent criterion (WCAG 2.2), and drag-only reordering is one of the places it's still most often missed — dragging feels so natural and effortless for a mouse user that the total absence of any alternative is genuinely easy to overlook during both design and review, right up until someone actually tries to reorder anything without a mouse.
Drag-only reordering excludes anyone who can't perform a continuous drag gesture — a single click-based alternative is what 2.5.7 requires, not the removal of drag as an option.

contentSections.title: Hover-only content excludes the same users, a different way

contentSections.body: A navigation menu reveals its submenu only on mouse hover — no click needed, but also no way to open it with a switch or voice command, since "hover" isn't a discrete activation event those tools can trigger. Switch access selects and activates; it doesn't hover. Voice control can sometimes simulate a hover, but unreliably and slowly, and most users never learn the specific command exists.

contentSections.scenario: The same hover-only submenu, tested with a plain keyboard: Tab reaches the parent menu item, but nothing opens the submenu without an actual mouseover event.
contentSections.question: Beyond the switch/voice problem, what has this design also failed?

options.label: Keyboard operability entirely — a submenu that opens purely on :hover, with no click, focus, or Enter alternative, excludes keyboard users too, not just switch and voice users
Nothing else — this is purely a switch/voice-specific issue and keyboard users are unaffected
This only matters for screen reader users specifically

feedback.keyboardtoo: Right, and this connects directly back to the keyboard module: focus and hover are two different events entirely. Tab moves focus; it never simulates a mouseover. Anything gated purely behind :hover excludes every non-mouse input method simultaneously — keyboard, switch and voice users all hit the identical wall for the identical reason.
feedback.onlyswitch: Keyboard users are affected too — Tab reaching the parent item proves focus works, but nothing about focus triggers a :hover-only reveal, which is exactly the gap this concept-flow is surfacing.
feedback.onlysr: This is specifically an operability problem (can the submenu be opened at all), not an announcement problem — a screen reader user using a mouse would actually be able to trigger this hover just fine; it's every non-mouse input method that's excluded.

contentSections.concept: **A single :hover-only trigger excludes every input method that isn't a mouse, all at once — keyboard, switch, and voice users share the identical wall.** This is the same lesson the keyboard module opened with, resurfacing here: focus and hover have always been two separate events, and confusing them (or building only for one) is one of the most common single causes of a whole class of exclusions across this entire phase.

contentSections.body: The fix pattern: trigger the same content on both hover and focus (`:hover, :focus-within` in CSS, or a click-to-toggle pattern that works well for touch too), and per WCAG 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus, make sure hover-revealed content is dismissible (Escape), remains visible while the pointer moves onto it, and doesn't vanish the instant it appears — three separate, specific sub-requirements once hover-revealed content exists at all, not just "also trigger it on focus."
Hover-only interactions don't just exclude switch and voice users — they almost always fail keyboard users too, because Tab moves focus, and focus was never the same event as hover.

title: Lab — Review One Interface for Switch and Voice Operation
description: Pick one real, interactive interface and put it through everything this module covers: scan-order cost, target size, voice-name reachability, timing, and drag/hover alternatives.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate a real interface's switch-scanning cost and voice-control reachability
Identify every control with no usable accessible name for voice control
Write a review naming every unnameable control and every timing barrier with a concrete fix

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: One real interface, checked against every mechanism this module named — scan order, target size, voice-name reachability, timing, drag and hover — because a single interface rarely fails just one of them.

contentSections.title: Switch and voice operation review
contentSections.brief: Pick one real, interactive interface — a settings page, a form, a list you can reorder or filter. If you have access to real switch-access or voice-control software, use it directly; if not, simulate switch scanning by tabbing through the interface in strict linear order and timing yourself, and simulate voice control by reading the accessible name of every control (via devtools) and checking whether you could say something short and unambiguous to reach each one.
contentSections.deliverable: A review naming every control with no usable accessible name (unreachable by voice), every point where scan order or control count creates a real cost, and every timing or drag/hover barrier — each with a concrete fix.

stages.title: Map the interface and estimate scan cost
stages.instructions: List every interactive control on the interface in order. Note roughly how many scan-steps a switch user would need to reach the least-accessible one, and whether any real grouping (headings, fieldsets, landmarks) exists to shortcut that cost. Measure at least five targets' sizes and spacing against the 24px/spacing-exception rule from this module.
stages.checkpoint: You have a full control inventory, an estimated worst-case scan cost, and target-size measurements for at least five controls.

stages.title: Check voice-control reachability
stages.instructions: For every control, read its actual computed accessible name (devtools, from the semantics module). Note anything with no name, a generic name ("button"), or a name duplicated across multiple controls — all three make a control unreachable or ambiguous by voice, for the reasons this module covered.
stages.checkpoint: Every control has a recorded accessible name, and every unnamed, generic, or duplicated one is flagged.

stages.title: Check timing, drag and hover
stages.instructions: Note any time limit on the interface and whether it can be turned off, extended, or comes with a warning. Test any drag-based interaction for a single-pointer alternative. Test any hover-revealed content with the mouse away entirely — does it ever appear, and if it does appear another way, does it stay dismissible and stick around while the pointer moves onto it?
stages.checkpoint: Timing, drag and hover have each been explicitly tested, with a finding or a confirmed pass for each.

stages.title: Write the review and self-check
stages.instructions: Write up every finding with its specific location, why it excludes the specific input method it does, and a concrete fix. Order by real-world cost — a completely unreachable action outranks a merely slow one. Then run the self-check against the rubric.
stages.checkpoint: The review is ordered by real cost, and every finding has a specific fix a developer could act on without further investigation.

rubric.criterion: Scan cost was actually estimated, not just described as "probably slow"
rubric.meets: A rough step count or comparable measure is given for the interface's least-accessible control, tied to whether real grouping exists.

rubric.criterion: Every control's accessible name was checked, not assumed from its visible label
rubric.meets: Names were read from the computed accessibility tree, and every missing, generic or duplicated one is flagged specifically.

rubric.criterion: Timing, drag and hover were each explicitly tested
rubric.meets: The report states a specific finding or a confirmed pass for all three, not silence implying nothing was found.

rubric.criterion: Every finding names which input method it excludes and why
rubric.meets: A finding says more than "this is inaccessible" — it names switch, voice, or both, and the specific mechanism.

rubric.criterion: Fixes are concrete, not generic
rubric.meets: "Add aria-label distinguishing each product" rather than "improve accessibility."

contentSections.body: A single interface rarely fails just one of these mechanisms — checking all five in one pass is what a real switch-and-voice review actually looks like, not five separate audits.

questions.explanation: Voice control depends on exactly the same accessible-name computation a screen reader does — an unnamed control is unreachable to both, for the same underlying reason.

questions.from: This module — Switch Access and Voice Control
questions.prompt: A navigation submenu opens only on mouse :hover, with no click or focus alternative. Besides switch and voice users, who else does this exclude?

options.label: Keyboard users — Tab moves focus, which was never the same event as a mouse hover
Nobody else — this is purely a switch/voice-specific issue
Only users on touchscreens

questions.explanation: A hover-only trigger excludes every non-mouse input method at once — keyboard, switch and voice users all hit the same wall, because focus and hover are genuinely separate events.

questions.from: Previous module — Magnification, Zoom and Low Vision
questions.prompt: A page requires horizontal scrolling to read ordinary text at 400% zoom. What does this fail?

options.label: WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow
Nothing — some horizontal scrolling is expected at high zoom
WCAG 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap

questions.explanation: 1.4.10 Reflow specifically prohibits a second, horizontal scroll axis for ordinary content at 400% zoom.

questions.from: Previous module — Magnification, Zoom and Low Vision
questions.prompt: Two status colors both individually pass 4.5:1 contrast against their background, and color is the only thing distinguishing the two states. Is that sufficient?

options.label: No — WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color requires a non-color signal too, independent of contrast ratio
Yes — passing contrast is the only relevant requirement
No — the ratios simply need to be higher

questions.explanation: Contrast ratio and use of color are separate criteria — a colorblind user may not distinguish the colors regardless of how well each passes individually.

questions.from: Previous module — Magnification, Zoom and Low Vision
questions.prompt: A checkbox's checked state is shown purely with a background-color fill. What happens under forced-colours mode?

options.label: Checked and unchecked become visually identical, since background-color is exactly what the OS overrides
Nothing changes — forced colours only affects text
The checkbox stops being clickable

questions.explanation: background-color is precisely the property forced-colours mode overrides — with no border or icon as a fallback signal, the states become indistinguishable.

questions.from: Older module — Screen Readers: Actually Using One
questions.prompt: Why does a visually obvious update, like a price change, sometimes produce zero screen reader announcement?

options.label: A screen reader only announces what has focus or what's inside a live region — a plain DOM update elsewhere is silent by default
This only happens on outdated screen reader versions
Updates are always announced automatically regardless of focus

questions.explanation: Silence is the default for anything outside current focus — the same underlying gap the timing and drag/hover lessons in this module also depend on fixing with a focus move.

questions.from: Older module — Semantics, Roles and the Accessibility Tree
questions.prompt: A div with an onclick handler and visible text reading "Save" — what role does it expose in the accessibility tree?

options.label: No implicit role at all — divs carry none, regardless of click handlers or text content
button, because the visible text reads like one
link, the default for anything clickable

questions.explanation: A div carries no implicit role under any circumstance — this is exactly why a div-based control needs explicit role and accessible-name work before voice control (or a screen reader) can reach it at all.

questions.from: Older module — Semantics, Roles and the Accessibility Tree
questions.prompt: A field has both a correctly connected native label AND a leftover aria-label with different, older text. Which one wins the accessible name?

options.label: The aria-label — it sits higher in the accessible-name priority order and fully overrides native labeling
The native label, since it's programmatically correct
Whichever appears first in the HTML source

questions.explanation: aria-label wins outright — and since voice control reads this same computed name, a stale aria-label can silently break voice reachability too, not just screen reader accuracy.
